nameStory: The spotted hake gets its name from the distinctive spots or blotches that pattern its body, helping distinguish it from its plainer cousins. The word 'hake' comes from an old English word meaning 'hook,' likely referring to the sharp teeth these fish use to catch prey.
description: The spotted hake is a slender, elongated bottom-dwelling fish that belongs to the cod family. It has a tapering body that gets narrower toward the tail, giving it an almost eel-like appearance. These fish typically grow to about 12-16 inches long, though some can reach up to 2 feet. Their most notable feature is the pattern of dark spots or blotches scattered across their brownish or grayish body.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Look for dark brown or black spots scattered across a brownish-gray body that feels smooth and slightly slimy to the touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Long, slender body that tapers dramatically toward the tail, feeling firm but flexible when handled

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two dorsal fins on top - a short triangular one in front and a very long one that runs most of the way down the back

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large mouth positioned at the front of the head with small, sharp teeth that feel rough against your finger

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Usually 12-16 inches long, fitting comfortably in two hands when caught

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found on sandy or muddy bottoms in deeper coastal waters, often hiding partially buried during the day

habitat: Spotted hake live in the deeper coastal waters of New England, typically on sandy or muddy bottoms where they can partially bury themselves. They prefer waters 50-300 feet deep along the continental shelf. You'll find them from the Gulf of Maine down to southern New England waters, often in areas where the bottom transitions from sand to mud.

seasonality.spring: Spotted hake begin moving into slightly shallower waters as temperatures warm, becoming more active after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be caught by anglers, actively feeding in warmer waters.
seasonality.fall: Fish remain active but begin moving to deeper waters as temperatures drop, often caught during bottom fishing expeditions.
seasonality.winter: Retreat to deeper, more stable waters where they're less active and harder to locate.

funFact: Spotted hake can actually 'walk' along the ocean floor using their pelvic fins like little legs, which have evolved into thread-like appendages that help them feel around for food in the dark depths!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with red hake and white hake, but the spotted hake's distinctive dark spots are the giveaway - neither of its cousins has this clear spotting pattern. Remember: spots equal spotted hake!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'hake,' these fish are actually more closely related to cod than to true hakes, which is why you might see them grouped with other cod-family fish in field guides or at fish markets.
compareHints: Unlike red hake which has a reddish tint and white hake which is more uniformly colored, spotted hake is the only one in the genus with distinct dark spots. Red hake tends to be smaller and more reddish, while white hake is larger and lacks any distinctive markings, making spotted hake the 'middle child' with the most obvious field marks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red hake can be distinguished from their close relatives by color - they're much more reddish than the grayish white hake or the spotted pattern of spotted hake.
White Hake is the palest of the three Urophycis species in New England waters - much lighter than the reddish-brown Red Hake and lacking the distinctive spots of the Spotted Hake.
